opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting long-term payoffs of interpretability, even though it's not the main reason we do it day to day.

Neuroscientists have spent over a century trying to understand the brain under brutal constraints. You can record from a handful of neurons, or get very coarse signals from fMRI or EEG. You can't freely intervene, you can't copy the brain and run controlled experiments, and you can't look at every connection at once. It's like trying to reverse-engineer a computer by putting a few probes on the motherboard while it runs.

With neural networks, we have the opposite situation. We can see every weight and every activation. We can ablate parts, steer them, and rerun the exact same input a million times. So we can actually develop and test the tools of "neuroscience" in a setting where we get ground truth. If a method for finding features or circuits doesn't work on a model where we can see everything, it's probably not going to work on a brain.

There's also growing evidence that these systems converge on similar representations to ours. Vision models learn edge detectors and curve detectors that look a lot like what we see in early visual cortex. Language models develop representations that line up surprisingly well with activity in human language areas. There's this idea that different learning systems trained on the same world end up discovering similar structure. If that holds, then understanding how a model represents concepts, like how it handles superposition, packing many more concepts than it has neurons, could give us real hypotheses about how the brain does the same thing.

I want to be careful, though. These models are not brains. The architectures, learning rules, and energy constraints are very different, so you can't just transfer findings directly. What I think we can do is build a science of how intelligent systems represent and compute things in general. Brains and neural networks would both be examples within that broader science, and right now neural networks are by far the easier one to study.

So my hope is that interpretability becomes a kind of model organism for cognition, the way fruit flies or mice are for biology. We figure out the principles where we can see everything, and then go look for them in the much harder case of the human mind.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few layers to that. The honest answer is that neural networks and brains are very different substrates, and I'd be cautious about anyone who claims that what we find inside a transformer maps one-to-one onto what's happening in a cortex. But I do think there's something real here, and it comes from the fact that for the first time we have a system that does something like language, something like reasoning, that we can fully open up and inspect.

With the brain, neuroscience has always been constrained by access. You get a handful of electrodes, or fMRI at a resolution of millions of neurons per voxel, and you're trying to reverse-engineer the whole thing from that. With a neural network, we have every weight, every activation, and we can intervene on any of them. So it becomes a kind of model organism. Not because it is a brain, but because it's a system that learned to do intelligent-seeming things from data, and we can ask: what kinds of representations does that process produce? What kinds of structure emerge when you optimize for prediction?

And some of what we've found, I think, is suggestive. Things like superposition, where a network represents far more concepts than it has dimensions by overlapping them. Or the way that features compose into circuits that implement algorithms. Those are not obviously brain-specific or silicon-specific facts. They might be facts about what any learning system has to do when it's under pressure to compress a messy world into a finite set of parameters. If that's true, then understanding them in the artificial case gives neuroscientists hypotheses to go look for, with much better tooling than they'd have otherwise.

The other direction I find interesting is more conceptual. Working on interpretability forces you to get very precise about questions that are usually fuzzy. What does it mean for a system to "know" something? What's the difference between a representation and a computation? Where does a concept live? Those are old philosophy-of-mind questions, and they suddenly become engineering questions you can get empirical traction on. I think that discipline, of having to make the vague thing operational, is going to feed back into how we think about human cognition, even if the specific mechanisms turn out to be different.

So I'd frame it less as "neural networks will explain the brain" and more as "neural networks give us a second example of intelligence, and having two examples instead of one changes what questions you're even able to ask."

astra-6.text:
I think neural networks give us a way to make some of our intuitions about thought concrete. We say that people learn from experience, recognize patterns, or combine concepts—but how does that actually happen? With a neural network, you can watch a system learn and ask what representations it develops, what generalizes, and where it breaks down.

That doesn’t mean the brain works exactly like today’s models. But even the differences can be informative. If a model needs thousands of examples to learn something a person picks up from one or two, that gives us a sharper question: what is the person bringing to the task that the model is missing?

So I see these systems as a way to generate and test hypotheses about thought. The exciting part is moving from a metaphor about how the mind works to a mechanism we can actually investigate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think neural networks give us a way to make some of our intuitions about thought concrete. We can say that a person learns from experience or forms an internal representation of the world, but what does that actually mean? With a neural network, we can watch how learning changes a system and test what information its internal representations contain.

That doesn’t mean the brain works exactly like today’s models. But it gives us hypotheses we can investigate. How do concepts emerge? How does prior experience shape what we notice? Why does something generalize in one situation and fail in another? Understanding how those things happen in an artificial system could help us ask more precise questions about human thought—and understand which aspects require a different explanation.
